text: Computers only process numbers.
That might seem counterintuitive when you look at a screen full of text,
but behind the scenes,
those words are converted to numbers so the computer can work with them.
The same rule applies to AI.
Look at this simple chat.
You ask, what's the best Avengers movie?
In the AI answers, most people point to Avengers Endgame.
It's the big payoff to a decade of films and it broke box office records.
Infinity War is the other top pick if you like a darker ending.
You sent and received words.
How do those words become numbers and then turn back into words?
One obvious idea would be to assign each whole word in every language a unique number.
But that method breaks down almost immediately.
People are constantly inventing new slang, making typos,
and typing things like emojis or computer code.
Even a list of a million words couldn't cover everything a person might type into a prompt.
Human language expands continuously,
which requires AI to find a completely different way to process text.
Instead, AI uses reusable chunks of text called tokens.
Think of them as building blocks for language.
Here is what tokens look like.
In row one, unbelievable becomes un, believe, and vole.
One word, three chunks.
In the next rows, unusual and unmatchable both reuse the un-chunk.
Some split cleanly.
Row four's basketball becomes basket and ball.
Row six shows iHeartAI as three tokens with SP marking spaces.
Even the web address at the bottom breaks down into eight chunks.
By breaking text down into these reusable chunks rather than storing whole words,
AI creates a highly efficient system.
It can piece together any combination of letters or symbols you throw at it,
including words it has never seen before.
A token can be a whole word or just part of one.
The full collection of tokens is called the model's vocabulary.
Engineers build this vocabulary by running a program that analyzes
massive collections of text to identify the most frequent patterns.
Once that vocabulary is built, every single token is assigned a unique number.
This number is known as its token ID.
This introduces a major difference in how humans and machines read.
Looking at the left, when you see cat, you know what it means.
Fur whiskers the animal.
For AI, looking at the right,
the tokenizer converts the written word cat directly into ID 4719.
That numerical ID acts purely as a database address.
It tells the computer which chunk to retrieve,
but it holds no concept of what the object actually is.
A token ID identifies the token.
Meaning comes later.
Now we can map out exactly what happens when you hit send,
as shown in this three-step diagram.
In step one, you start with text by typing a message.
In step two, a tokenizer program takes your input
and splits that text into reusable chunks.
In step three, the tokenizer looks up the specific IDs for each chunk.
If we use unbelievable as our example,
the tokenizer searches its vocabulary to find that the ID for
un is 359, the ID for believe is 32898,
and the ID for bowl is 24694.
As the diagram summarizes, tokenization turns text
into token IDs the model can use.
When the model calculates its response,
that answer comes out strictly as token IDs.
The tokenizer steps in one last time to convert those numbers
back into their corresponding text chunks,
snapping them together into the readable sentences
that appear on your screen.
Words become numbers.
That lets AI work with your language using math.
